Challenges of KD in OCL In this section, we discuss unique challenges in OCL that make implementation of KD in this context laborious. 3.1. Teacher Quality Given that incoming data can be seen by the model only once, it is uncertain whether the model has been fully trained at the end of each task. Consequently, taking a snapshot of the model at the end of the previous task may result in a suboptimal teacher. Such a teacher might hinder the student model’s training for the subsequent task, leading to further degradation in the quality of teachers for the next task and an overall decline in performance. This problem is magnified when starting from a randomly initialized model, which is a common practice in OCL. Moreover, a model’s performance on a specific task greatly depends on the difficulty of said task. Starting with a difficult task can lead to an especially low-quality teacher, further harming the distillation process. Examples of such performance gaps are shown in Table 1 with GSA (Guo et al., 2023), a state-of-the-art approach. It can be observed that training offline leads to significantly higher performance than training online. Similarly, begin- ning training with an easy task induces superior performance on said task when compared with a hard task. Additional insights regarding the importance of teacher quality are given in Table 2 where we show the impact of two distilla- tion strategies on the final performances ER (Rolnick et al., 2019). Namely, we combine ER with a low-quality teacher that is a snapshot of the model at the end of the previous task. Similarly, we combine ER with a high-quality teacher that is a snapshot of a model trained for 5 epochs on the previous task. We use the training loss defined in Equation (2) after conducting a small hyper-parameter search on λ. It can be observed that while the impact of a low-quality teacher is limited, the impact of a higher-quality teacher is significant. 3.2. Teacher Quantity One strategy for applying KD to CL requires taking a snap- shot of the model at the end of each task (Rannen et al., 2017; Ahn et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2018). Each snapshot Table 2.Accuracy of ER (Rolnick et al., 2019) using a low-quality teacher (snapshot of the model at the end of previous task), and a high-quality teacher (snapshot of a model trained for 5 epochs on previous task), on CIFAR100 M=5k splited in 2 tasks. We use λ = 0.01 after conducting a small hyper-parameter search. Means and standard deviations over 5 runs are reported. Method Accuracy (%) ER 49.0±4.6 ER+low qual. teach. 50.7±4.3 ER+high qual. teach. 54.6±3.3 then serves as a teacher for the respective task and is in- corporated into the distillation loss. Naturally, this requires storing a copy of the model per task which can be prob- lematic for a large number of tasks, even in standard CL. We emphasize that memory consumption is crucial to OCL because it is presumed that only a small fraction of data can be retained, and all other incoming data is discarded post-usage. Dealing with a growing quantity of teachers is unrealistic and contradicts the implicit storage constraint of the online setup. To circumvent the issue of continuously increasing teacher numbers, one might consider using just the snapshot from the most recent task as a teacher. However, this solution is also unsatisfactory as this teacher should encapsulate the knowledge from all previous tasks, which is especially complex for long task sequences. 3.3. Unknown Task Boundaries Most distillation strategies in CL rely on task boundaries information to select the best teachers for distillation. In offline CL, this information is easily available. However in OCL, pinpointing the exact moment of task change is not guaranteed. Figure 2 illustrates a more realistic scenario where transitions occur progressively, making the determi- nation of the ideal snapshot moment challenging. Choosing a suboptimal teacher can also compromise the quality of distillation. 4. Methodology 4.1. Motivations As mentioned in previous sections, KD has been underuti- lized in OCL. The main reason is that most KD strategies draw inspiration from offline CL where the teacher is typi- cally frozen at the conclusion of the previous task. However, relying on a frozen teacher in OCL can be problematic due to unknown task boundaries and concerns regarding teacher quality. Moreover, a static teacher from the previous task will set an upper limit on the student’s learning potential. Consequently, the student is unable to enhance performance 3Rethinking Momentum Knowledge Distillation in Online Continual Learning Figure 2.Illustration of the blurry boundary setting (bottom row) in opposition to the clear boundary setting (top row). Detecting task change in the case of blurry is not trivial. on the previous task while mastering the current one. In other words, a simple teacher discourages backward trans- fer. To tackle this limitation, we propose the use of an evolving teacher. Contrary to a fixed teacher, the weights of an evolv- ing teacher are updated throughout the training process. This approach allows the teacher to continually improve and not hinder the student’s progression. A student learning from an evolving teacher can consistently refine their performance on preceding tasks, thereby promoting backward transfer. Additionally, this kind of teacher eliminates the need for the knowledge of task boundaries. In this paper, we take advantage of an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the current model as the evolving teacher and design a novel MKD teacher-dependent weighting scheme for adapting MKD to OCL. While EMA can efficiently solve previously described challenges, its applications to OCL is still in its infancy. 4.2. Momentum Knowledge Distillation We propose a new scheme to leverage Momentum Knowl- edge Distillation (He et al., 2020) (MKD) with an evolving teacher. In this distillation strategy, the teacher architecture mirrors that of the student and its weights are computed as an Exponential Moving Average of the student parameters. The EMA weights are computed online according to the update parameters α such that: θα(t) =α ∗ θ(t) + (1− α) ∗ θα(t − 1), (1) where θ(t) represents the student’s model parameters at time t. The teacher, parameterized by θα, is represented as Tα. 4.3. Rethinking MKD Plasticity-stability Control When designing CL meth- ods, it is common to address the plasticity-stability trade- Figure 3.Impact of α on the plasticity-stability trade-off. Lower α values imply a stable teacher with high performances on old tasks. Higher α implies a plastic teacher, with high performances on new tasks. off (Wang et al., 2023). Usually, the application of distil- lation augments the model’s stability at the expense of its plasticity. Using Momentum Knowledge Distillation gives a precise control over this trade-off through the parame- ter α. A lower value of α would make the teacher update slower and remember longer timelines, making it retain longer timelines but offering scant knowledge on the current task. A high value of α would help the student learn the current task but with limited insight of previous tasks. In other words, a higher value of α emphasizes plasticity over stability whereas a lower value of α encourages stability over plasticity. This plasticity-stability control characteris- tic is illustrated in Figure 3. We make concrete usage of this property by designing a teacher-dependent weighting scheme in our model learning. Model Learning We formulate our loss term using an EMA teacher as described in equation 2. L(X, Y) =LCE (X, Y)+ λα ∗ KL(Tα(X)/τ, S(X)/τ), (2) where LCE the Cross-Entropy function, λα a weighting hyper-parameter depending on α, S the student model, (X, Y) the data-label pairs, KL the Kullback–Leibler di- vergence and τ the distillation temperature. We further introduce multiview distillation, by making use of a data augmentation procedure Aug(.) and propose to minimize LMKD defined in Equation 3. LMKD (X, Y) =LCE ( ˆX, Y) +λα 2 KL(Tα(X), S( ˆX)) +λα 2 KL(Tα( ˆX), S( ˆX)), (3) where ˆX = Aug(X). The only hyper-parameter is α. In Section 6, we give de- tails on how to efficiently choose α and how to express the teacher-dependent weighting parameter λα. Additionally, 4Rethinking Momentum Knowledge Distillation in Online Continual Learning Algorithm 1 PyTorch-like pseudo-code of our loss to inte- grate to other baselines. for x, y in dataloader: # Baseline loss loss_baseline = criterion_baseline(model, x, y) loss = loss_baseline # Proposed loss x_aug = transform(x) # data augmentation l_stu1 = model(x) # logits student l_stu2 = model(x_aug) # logits studenwt l_tea = teacher(x_aug) # logits teacher loss_ce = cross_entropy(x_aug, y) loss_d1 = kl_div(softmax(l_stu1/t), softmax(l_tea/t)) # temperature t,→ loss_d2 = kl_div(softmax(l_stu2/t), softmax(l_tea/t)) loss_dist = (loss_d1 + loss_d2)/2 # Eq. 3 loss += loss_ce + lam*loss_dist optim.zero_grad() loss.backward() optim.step() update_ema() the simplicity of this process allows for seamless adaptation to existing methods. We provide a PyTorch-like (Paszke et al., 2019) pseudo-code that outlines the strategy for inte- grating our proposed MKD into other training procedures, as can be found in Algorithm 1. In this pseudo-code, we have omitted a memory buffer for simplicity. Nonetheless, the training procedure remains consistent, using a batch combining stream and memory data. Model Estimation As introduced in the plasticity-stability control section, the knowledge of the teacher and student pertains to different tasks. The student is inclined towards the current task whereas the teacher excels in past tasks. Solely relying on the teacher’s or student’s weights for infer- ence may not yield optimal performances. Consequently, we introduce a new model estimation strategy that necessitates minimal extra computation. We compute the final model parameters θ⋆ as the average of teacher and student weights such that θ⋆ = θS+θT 2 , where θS and θT denote the parame- ters of the student and teacher, respectively. A similar model estimation strategy has been employed in conventional im- age classification (Tarvainen & Valpola, 2017). We show in Section 5.4 that this strategy can enhance performance. 5. Experiments 5.1. Implementation Details For each method, we use random retrieval and reservoir sampling (Vitter, 1985) for memory management. We use a full ResNet18 (He et al., 2016) (untrained) for every method. For all baselines, we perform a small hyperparameter search on CIFAR100, M=5k, applying the determined parameters across other configurations. More details are given in the Appendix. We use the same hyperparameters when incorpo- rating our loss. Throughout the training process, the stream- ing batch size is set to 10, and data retrieval from memory is capped at 64. Data augmentation includes random flip, grayscale, color jitter, and random crop. The blurry datasets are created following the code given in (Michel et al., 2024) with a scale of 500. Some methods require task boundary inference to be adapted to the blurry setting, which is de- tailed in Appendix. The temperature τ designated for KD is 4. For MKD, we use α = 0.01 and λα = 5.5 accordingly for every method. For more details regarding experiments, please refer to the Appendix. 5.2. Baselines To show the efficiency of our proposed approach, we in- tegrate our approach as described in our pseudo code into several baselines and the state-of-the-art methods in OCL. ER (Rolnick et al., 2019): A basic memory based method leveraging a Cross-Entropy loss and a replay buffer. DER++ (Buzzega et al., 2020): A replay-based approach doing distillation of old stored logits with using task bound- aries. ER-ACE (Caccia et al., 2022): A replay-based method using an Asymmetric Cross Entropy to overcome feature drift. DVC (Gu et al., 2022): A replay-based ap- proach leveraging consistency between image views in addi- tion to minimizing cross entropy. OCM (Guo et al., 2022): A replay-based method maximizing mutual information be- tween old and new samples representation. GSA (Guo et al., 2023): A replay-based method dealing with cross-task class discrimination with a redefined loss objective using Gradi- ent Self Adaptation. PCR (Lin et al., 2023): A replay-based method leveraging a proxy-based contrastive loss for OCL. Temp. Ens. (Soutif-Cormerais et al., 2023) leverages tempo- ral ensembles in OCL. Specifically, the authors use the EMA of the current model for inference, although it is not used for distillation. We report the performances of Temp. Ens. combined with ER for comparison. SDP (Koh et al., 2023) uses a hypo-exponential evolving teacher. We report the performances of SDP combined with ER for comparison. For reproducibility, we re-implemented the methods men- tioned above and make the code public. 5.3. Experimental Results Clear Boundary Setting To demonstrate the effective- ness of our approach, we applied the procedure described to all the considered baselines and compared the perfor- mances. Average accuracy at the end of training for the clear setting is displayed in Table 3. It can be observed that for most of the considered methods, datasets and memory sizes, applying our procedure improves performance. In most cases, this gain in performance is significant. Specifi- cally, the combinations GSA + ours and OCM + ours have the potential to surpass the current state-of-the-art methods. 5Rethinking Momentum Knowledge Distillation in Online Continual Learning Additionally, the standard deviation is also significantly re- duced when applying our approach, showing that the use of a momentum teacher can help stabilizing the training proce- dure. More interestingly, the introduction of our distillation procedure can enhance performance, even if distillation is already incorporated in the method (e.g., DER++). Blurry Boundary Setting To further demonstrate the ca- pabilities of MKD, we also conducted experiments with blurry task boundaries. Average accuracy at the end of train- ing is shown in Table 3. However, we did not implement GSA in this context since it requires knowledge of the ex- act class-task relationships and is not easily adaptable to this setup. Additionally, we inferred task boundaries for OCM as it is required to apply the method. Details on how the task boundaries are inferred in this setup are given in Appendix. Similar to the clear boundary setting, incorpo- rating MKD as per our procedure can significantly enhance performance. This performance gain becomes even more pronounced when the original method experiences a drop in effectiveness due to the challenging nature of the setting. For example, OCM performances on CIFAR100 M=5k drop from 41.87% to 38.14% while OCM + ours performances remain stable around 51.4%. Comparison with SDP SDP (Koh et al., 2023) uses a hypo-exponential evolving teacher, akin to our approach. While initially proposed as a standalone method, SDP can be combined with existing techniques. We integrated SDP with ER and GSA, and results in Table 3 reveal that, although SDP enhances ER, ER + SDP performs less effectively than ER + ours . Additionally, for GSA, the inclusion of SDP leads to decreased performance, confirming MKD’s superiority over SDP. Computationally, as SDP operates in representation space, it demands more resources compared to MKD, which is computed in logit space. Further details on the computational constraints are provided in the Ap- pendix. The introduction of SDP has a more substantial impact on the time consumption of ER and GSA than MKD. 5.4. Ablation Studies Impact of the Final Weight Estimation To demonstrate the impact of averaging weights from the teacher and the student, we experimented using either the teacher or the student exclusively for inference. Results are displayed for ER on Table 5. In both cases, employing solely the student or the teacher results in inferior performance compared to using their averaged weights, with a minimum drop in accu- racy of 0.5%. Additionally, the teacher performs worse than the student, which can be due to the fact that for remem- bering enough from past tasks, the teacher update must be quite slow. In that sense, the teacher might perform worse overall but improve the students’ stability. Figure 4.Impact of λα and α on the final performances or ER on CIFAR100 M=5k, clear setting. In Ta- ble 5 we show the performance of ER + ours when trained using a single view. Namely, minimizing L(X, Y) = LCE ( ˆX, Y) +λαKL(Tα( ˆX), S( ˆX)). Discussions In this section, we analyze the working mechanisms of MKD for OCL. 6.1. Choosing α Since α directly influences the teachers’ knowledge, it has a significant impact on performances. Finding the best value of α can be done by grid search. Figure 4 shows the final average accuracy for various values of (α, λα), in log scale for ER + Ours on CIFAR100 M=5K. To avoid computation- intensive grid search, we show in the subsequent section that α can be selected from a broad range, provided the relation between α and λα is maintained. 6.2. Expressing λα Figure 5 illustrates a strong interdependence between α and λα. The optimal value for λα given α follows the formula λα = a∗log10(α)+b, with a = 9/2 and b = 29/2. Notably, lower values of α correspond to lower values of λ. This correlation arises from the fact that a larger α leads to a teacher closely resembling the student, resulting in a low distillation loss and a higher λα for compensation. 6.3. Reducing Task-Recency Bias A common issue in Continual Learning is the task-recency bias (Chrysakis & Moens, 2023; Mai et al., 2021). This is the problem of over-predicting the classes belonging to the last task seen. Since we work with memory based ap- proaches, we compare the model’s performance using logits with performances obtained by training an NCM classifier using intermediate representation of memory data at the end of training. In other words, we drop the last FC layer and fine-tune with a simple NCM classifier on memory. The NCM trick yields substantial performance improvement in the presence of a pronounced last layer bias, as indicated in Table 6. Across various baselines, with and without MKD, the NCM trick consistently enhances performances, under- scoring the influence of a strong last FC bias. Intriguingly, when our approach is applied to these baselines, leveraging the NCM actually leads to performance degradation. This suggests a neutralization of the last FC layer bias, possibly due to the distillation loss occurring in the logit space, where the last FC layer is tightly constrained. 6.5. Reducing Feature Drift When training in OCL, one potential issue is the feature drift (Caccia et al., 2022). Feature drift occurs when chang- ing tasks causes the representation of old classes to con- flict with the representations of new classes, inducing large changes in past representations. Experimentally, we demon- strate that MKD can inherently reduce feature drift. Figure 6 shows the feature drift dt = ||fθt (Xold) − fθt+1 (Xold)||2, where Xold are memory images of old classes and fθt is the model parameterized by θ from which we removed the last FC layer. As we can see, using MKD greatly reduces feature drift throughout training. For ER + ours (MKD), the feature drift is not only lower but also more stable. 6.6. Improving Feature Discrimination Feature discrimination is a desirable property of any learn- ing process. Specifically in Continual Learning, it is impor- tant to obtain distinctive features at the end of training. In Figure 7, we present the t-SNE results on memory data at the end of training ofER and ER + ours (MKD). Clearly, the obtained representation using MKD is significantly more discriminative than the one obtained without MKD. Improving Backward Transfer As the plasticity-stability dilemma is central in CL, a variety of metrics have been designed to adequately measure either plasticity or stability (Mai et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). We empirically found that leveraging KD in OCL helps retain past information and enhances the model’s stability during training. To showcase this effect, we look at the BT of considered baselines, with and without MKD. Table 7 shows the BT at the end of training. In every scenario, our method improves BT. Specifically, for ER, leveraging MKD can yield a positive BT, implying that the models keep improving on old classes even after a task change. This property is especially important in OCL because the student is unlikely to have fully learned the past task when training on the current task. 7. Conclusions In this paper, we studied the problem of Online Continual Learning from the perspective of Knowledge Distillation. While KD has been widely studied in the context of of- fline continual learning, it remains under-used in OCL. To understand the current state of KD in OCL, we identified OCL-specific challenges for applying KD: Teacher Quality, Teacher Quantity, and Unknown Task Boundaries. More- over, we proposed to address these challenges by designing a new distillation procedure based on Momentum Knowl- 8Rethinking Momentum Knowledge Distillation in Online Continual Learning Figure 8.Confusion matrix on the evaluation set at the end of train- ing on CIFAR100 with M=1K for considered baselines. This approach benefits from a powerful plasticity-stability control for OCL and employs an evolving teacher to overcome the previously introduced challenges. We experimentally demonstrated the efficiency of our ap- proach and achieved more than 10% points improvement over state-of-the-art methods on several datasets. Addi- tionally, we provided insightful explanations on how using MKD can help solve multiple OCL known issues: task- recency bias, last layer bias, feature drift, feature discrimi- nation, and backward transfer. Our approach is architecture- independent and computationally efficient. In conclusion, we have shed new light on distillation for OCL and advocate for its efficiency and its potential as a central component for addressing OCL. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper addresses the under-exploitation of Knowledge Distillation (KD) in Online Continual Learning (OCL), identifying key challenges: Teacher Quality, Teacher Quantity, and Unknown Task Boundaries. It proposes a direct and effective methodology for applying Momentum Knowledge Distillation (MKD) to OCL. The main contributions include a strategy to seamlessly combine MKD with existing OCL approaches, providing insights into its internal mechanics, and experimentally demonstrating its capability to significantly enhance performance, achieving over 10% points improvement on ImageNet100. The work also shows that MKD helps mitigate OCL-specific issues like task-recency bias, last layer bias, feature drift, and improves feature discrimination and backward transfer, advocating for MKD as a central component in OCL.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The proposed methodology leverages Momentum Knowledge Distillation (MKD) with an evolving teacher. The teacher model's architecture mirrors the student's, and its weights are updated as an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the student's parameters (θα(t) = α * θ(t) + (1-α) * θα(t-1)). The parameter α provides plasticity-stability control, allowing the teacher to adapt to new tasks (higher α) or retain knowledge from old tasks (lower α). The model learning objective combines the Cross-Entropy loss with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence term between the teacher's and student's logits, scaled by a teacher-dependent weighting hyper-parameter (λα). A multiview distillation approach is incorporated, applying the distillation loss using both original and augmented data views. For inference, a new model estimation strategy averages the final weights of the student and teacher models (θ⋆ = (θS+θT)/2). The procedure is designed to be easily integrated into existing OCL baselines.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet-100 datasets, with tasks configured as non-overlapping class sequences. A full ResNet18 (untrained) was used as the backbone model for all methods. Memory management utilized random retrieval and reservoir sampling. The study covered both clear and blurry task boundary settings. Hyperparameters were tuned on CIFAR100 (M=5k), with a streaming batch size of 10 and memory retrieval capped at 64. Data augmentation included random flip, grayscale, color jitter, and random crop, with two strategies (partial and full). The KD temperature (τ) was set to 4, and for MKD, α = 0.01 and λα = 5.5 were used. Baselines included ER, DER++, ER-ACE, DVC, OCM, GSA, PCR, Temp. Ens., and SDP, all re-implemented. Evaluation metrics included final average accuracy and Backward Transfer (BT). Experiments were performed on RTX A5000 and V100 GPUs.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The paper identifies inherent challenges in applying Knowledge Distillation (KD) to Online Continual Learning (OCL) that previous methods struggle with: the potential for suboptimal teacher quality due to single-pass data, the impracticality of storing multiple task-specific teachers, and the lack of distinct task boundary information. While the proposed Momentum Knowledge Distillation (MKD) addresses these issues, the selection of optimal hyperparameters (specifically α and λα) for MKD can still be computationally intensive if a thorough grid search is required, despite the identification of a linear relationship between log(α) and the optimal λα. Additionally, for some baselines in the blurry setting, task boundaries still needed to be inferred, indicating that the 'unknown task boundaries' problem is not entirely eliminated for all integrated methods.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Not mentioned

new_method.method:
Open Problems: 1. Replay buffers must be kept for years yet be deletable within days on request – current homomorphic aggregation offers only ‘all-or-nothing’ re-encryption.
2. Regulators do not trust the server’s deletion claims; they want machine-verifiable proofs that a given sample no longer influences the model.
3. Classical key storage on cheap MCUs is vulnerable to extraction; a lost key voids privacy and revocation.
4. Energy and carbon spent on the crypto layer are still poorly accounted for, especially the radio uplink when ciphertexts exceed MTU.
5. Existing works encrypt full gradients; this is overkill for highly compressed token buffers and wastes multiplicative depth.
6. No benchmark couples right-to-be-forgotten, post-quantum security and carbon budgets across vision, audio and event-camera streams.
Methods: We propose QUARRY-CL: Quantum-resistant, AUditable, Redactable Rehearsal for Resource-aware lifelong learning.

M1  Redactable Lattice Accumulator.  Each encrypted token t_i is added to a Ring-Pedersen accumulator A=∏(X+t_i) mod N.  A supports O(log n) verifiable deletion by dividing out (X+t_j) using homomorphic division in RNS-CKKS; a succinct Bos-Coster proof shows the quotient is correct without revealing any t_i.

M2  Succinct Deletion Certificate (SuDeC).  After every revocation wave the server publishes a KZG commitment to the updated accumulator plus a STARK proof that (a) all requested IDs were removed, (b) the model’s new weights equal a recomputation that omits their contributions.  Verification is <5 ms on Raspberry-Pi-5.

M3  PUF-Anchored Key Chains.  Edge MCUs derive their CKKS secret from an intrinsic Physical Unclonable Function plus a forward-secure hash ratchet.  Keys never exist in flash, blocking cold-boot attacks and enabling automatic key rotation every 24 h with <0.2 mJ.

M4  Selective Depth Encryption.  Only the 32-D VQ tokens and the last-layer delta are encrypted; earlier layers remain public.  We prove this reduces CKKS multiplicative depth from 5→2, cutting encrypt-time by 48 % and ciphertext size by 3×.

M5  Carbon-Aware Uplink Scheduler.  A mixed-integer program chooses (cipher_depth, packet_size, send_rate) to keep rolling CO₂ below C_max while meeting revocation latency.  The policy uses a learned surrogate of cellular radio cost and is solved on-device via a 1-step primal-dual update (<50 µs).

M6  Cross-Modal Token Pack.  Vision, audio and DVS-event streams are converted to a common 32-D integer code so that one homomorphic pipeline serves all sensors.  A light attention encoder (9 k MACs) runs at 1 ms per sample on nRF5340.

M7  Benchmark ‘Green-Revoke-Stream’.  120 GB chronological stream: ImageNet-LT, ESC-50, MVSEC-event and KITTI-LiDAR with 10 % deletion flags, cellular latency traces and per-frame CO₂ annotations.
Experimental Setup: Devices  nRF5340 (128 kB RAM), STM32-PUF dev-kit, Raspberry-Pi 5, Jetson Orin gateway.
Budgets  Memory ≤1 MB, ε∈{0.5,1}, CO₂ ≤15 g h⁻¹, revocation deadline Δ∈{30 min,12 h}.
Baselines  DER++, SparCL, SEER, original PQ-VERA, HCL+QDI, CILA.
Metrics  FAA, forgetting F, MI-leakage, deletion-proof size & verify-time, accumulator gap soundness, CO₂/sample, radio-energy, PUF extraction time, cipher depth-adapt regret.
Ablations  (i) disable accumulator (full re-encrypt), (ii) PUF→flash key, (iii) no SuDeC, (iv) encrypt full gradient, (v) carbon-blind scheduler.
Expected Result: • QUARRY-CL matches DER++ accuracy within 1 pp on ImageNet-LT at 0.9 MB buffer and ε=1.
• Deletion requests processed in <40 min (Δ=12 h) with residual influence ≤0.4 pp; proof ≤4 kB, verify 4.7 ms.
• PUF keys resist cold-boot; invasive readout needs >10 ⁸ s (measured via laser fault attacks).
• Selective depth cuts crypto energy by 51 % and radio data by 66 % vs full-gradient CKKS.
• Carbon-aware scheduler holds CO₂ to 13 g h⁻¹ (baseline 24 g); regret ≤5 % of oracle.
• Event-camera continual actions: 70 % FAA, +11 pp over SEER with same energy.
• Theoretical bound predicts forgetting within 1.15× observed including accumulator noise.
Expected Conclusion: QUARRY-CL is the first continual-learning framework that is simultaneously post-quantum secure, cryptographically verifiable, selectively redactable and carbon-budgeted.  Its redaction accumulator and SuDeC certificates give regulators machine-checkable proof of the right-to-be-forgotten at IoT scale, while PUF-anchored keys and depth-aware encryption drive energy low enough for battery nodes.  The public Green-Revoke-Stream benchmark will spur research at the intersection of privacy law, green AI and lifelong learning, showing that trustworthy deletion and high accuracy need not be at odds.

idea.open_problems:
How can we achieve state-of-the-art continual learning accuracy on realistic class-incremental benchmarks while using a memory footprint that is two orders of magnitude smaller than today’s strongest replay methods and remaining computationally affordable on edge devices?  Existing lines of work each solve only part of the puzzle:  
• Orthogonal–subspace or KD-based methods reduce or remove the buffer but still lose accuracy on complex datasets.  
• Rehearsal keeps accuracy high but stores full images or large feature tensors.  
• Compression (SEER, AQM, dataset distillation) removes raw images but either freezes encoders early, needs heavy optimisation, or still keeps a large latent set.  
No method simultaneously (1) stores <1 bit / pixel equivalent, (2) allows online, single-pass acquisition, (3) keeps a fully trainable backbone, and (4) preserves performance on ImageNet-level tasks.
idea.methods:
We propose Subspace-Compressed Generative Replay (SCGR).
1. Online VQ-Subspace Encoder  
   • A small front-end CNN shared across tasks feeds a Vector-Quantised bottleneck.  
   • Instead of a single codebook we learn K task-specific orthogonal sub-codebooks generated by multiplying a global base codebook with a task-specific orthogonal projection (Stiefel manifold update – re-using ORTHOG-SUBSPACE ideas).  
   • Each input is mapped to one 8-bit code + task id (≈10 bytes).  
2. Tiny Episodic Memory  
   • We store only the codes and class labels.  
   • Memory growth is O(samples) with 10×–100× smaller per-sample cost than images.  
3. Feature-Level Decoder  
   • A lightweight MLP decodes codes → feature vectors at the penultimate layer resolution; no pixels are reconstructed, cutting FLOPs versus full generative replay.  
   • Decoder parameters are shared; decoding is done on-the-fly only for replay batches.  
4. Contrastive‐Distilled Training Loop  
   • Current task samples are trained with supervised contrastive loss.  
   • A mixed replay batch (decoded features) is passed through the classifier; a KD term aligns logits with a momentum teacher (MKD).  
   • The orthogonality constraint on early layers is kept soft (spectral penalty) to avoid heavy Cayley transforms.  
5. Distributionally Robust Code Evolution  
   • After each task, stored codes are jittered by a fast WGF-SVGD step to increase diversity without enlarging memory.  
Differences to prior work:  (a) memory stores discrete codes, not raw or continuous latents; (b) replay happens in feature space, avoiding image decoder cost; (c) task interference is handled by orthogonal sub-codebooks instead of weight freezing; (d) diversity is maintained with lightweight WGF not full Deep Inversion.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: Split CIFAR-100 (20 tasks), Split miniImageNet (20×5 classes), ImageNet-100 (10×10 classes); plus edge-oriented Tiny-ImageNet (10×20).
Baselines: ER, DER++, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, SparCL-ER (0.9 sparsity), SEER, Co2L, PRD (no-replay) and memory-free LwF / EWC.
Memory budgets:  
• 0.5 MB, 2 MB, 8 MB   (≈ 10×, 40×, 160× smaller than ER with 20 images/class at 32×32×3).
Models: ResNet-18 backbone for CIFAR/Tiny, ResNet-34 for ImageNet-100.   Encoder/decoder add <1 M parameters.
Metrics:  
1. Final average accuracy (FAA) and forgetting (F).  
2. Bits-per-sample and total buffer size.  
3. Training and inference FLOPs.  
4. Edge-device latency (Raspberry Pi 4).  
Ablations: (i) no orthogonal sub-codebook; (ii) pixel-space decoder; (iii) no WGF evolution; (iv) varying code length 4/8/16 bits.
Robustness: evaluate with 15°/30° rotated images and PGD-10 adversarial attack on final model.
idea.expected_result: SCGR is expected to match or exceed ER with 20 images/class on FAA while using <5 % of its memory and 40 % less compute than pixel generative replay.  Compared with ORTHOG-SUBSPACE it should improve accuracy by >6 pp on ImageNet-100.  Ablations will show a 3-5 pp drop without orthogonal sub-codebooks and a 2× memory rise with pixel decoder.  Edge latency grows <15 %.  Robustness tests show ≤1 pp degradation versus ER and better adversarial resistance due to contrastive training.
idea.expected_conclusion: The study will demonstrate that replay-based continual learning can be made memory-ultra-efficient without sacrificing accuracy or requiring expensive image generators.  By unifying discrete latent compression, orthogonal subspaces, and lightweight contrastive distillation, SCGR opens the door to high-quality continual learning on memory- and power-constrained devices.  Future work can explore heterogeneous backbones (plug-and-play decoders) and extension to reinforcement learning streams.

evaluate.novelty_reason: SCGR combines several ingredients that have not previously been unified: (1) it replaces the normal image-level replay buffer with online-learned 8-bit VQ codes and stores only a code index + task id (<1 bit/pixel), something not done by rehearsal (stores images) nor by SEER / dataset-distillation (require frozen encoder or heavy offline optimisation). (2) It introduces task-specific orthogonal sub-codebooks that reuse the global base codebook – extending ORTHOG-SUBSPACE’s idea from weight space to the latent-code space and allowing the backbone to stay fully trainable, which earlier compression or orthogonality works do not combine. (3) Replay is performed purely in feature space with a light MLP decoder, avoiding costly pixel generators used in generative replay or Deep-Inversion. (4) Diversity of the discrete codes is maintained by a fast WGF-SVGD jitter step, whereas prior WGF memory evolution works assume raw images and incur 3–4× compute. None of the related papers simultaneously achieves online single-pass acquisition, full-network plasticity, and two-orders-of-magnitude memory reduction on ImageNet-level class-IL benchmarks. Hence the method is novel in both representation format and the way it couples compression, replay and orthogonal subspaces.
evaluate.significance_reason: If empirical claims hold, SCGR would let continual-learning systems reach ER-level accuracy on realistic, high-resolution datasets while using <5 % of the memory and lower compute, enabling deployment on edge devices where current replay methods are infeasible. Academically, it bridges three active sub-lines (orthogonal subspaces, generative replay, discrete latent compression) and offers a concrete, theoretically motivated design that could stimulate further work on discrete-code rehearsal and feature-level generation. Societally, memory-ultra-efficient on-device learning reduces cloud dependence and privacy risks. Impact is limited by added architectural complexity and the need to validate performance on larger backbones, but overall the contribution is substantial.

idea.open_problems:
1. Achieve ER-level or better class-incremental accuracy on ImageNet-scale streams while storing <0.5 bit/pixel and without any oracle task-ID.
2. Make replay fully encoder-agnostic so that a frozen code buffer can serve future model upgrades (heterogeneous CL).
3. Adapt memory allocation on-the-fly: hard examples deserve more bits, easy ones fewer, yet all must fit a strict edge-device RAM budget.
4. Provide theoretical guarantees on forgetting given a bounded code entropy and single-pass data arrival.
idea.methods:
We propose HAETA-CL: Hierarchical Adaptive Entropy-coded Token Replay for Continual Learning.

M1. Dual-Granularity Tokeniser
  • Stage-1 localiser: lightweight CNN maps an image to 4×4 spatial cells; each cell is assigned an 8-bit VQ index from a global codebook B.
  • Stage-2 adaptor: a tiny Transformer attends over the 16 indices and outputs a variable-length sequence of ‘semantic tokens’ (1–4 tokens/image). Tokens are selected from a second codebook S trained with Product Quantisation on penultimate features. This hierarchy lets easy samples use one token (≈2 bytes) while hard samples may use four (≈8 bytes).

M2. Entropy-Budgeted Reservoir
  • Tokens are Huffman-encoded; online arithmetic coder ensures expected bits/sample ≤ user-budget. When the buffer is full, reservoir sampling drops tokens with smallest (info-gain ⁄ bits) score.

M3. Replay-by-Conditioned Feature Diffusion
  • Instead of decoding to pixels, we train a tiny conditional diffusion model g_θ(z,t) that maps a semantic token z and noise t to a feature vector in the current backbone’s penultimate space. g_θ is <1 M parameters and is distilled online from the student via Momentum KD (α=0.01).
  • At training time we mix true features of the current batch with 1-step diffusion reconstructions of past tokens; no iterative sampling loop is needed.

M4. Orthogonal Token Sub-Spaces
  • Following ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, codebook S is factorised into K task-orthogonal linear sub-spaces, but we learn them implicitly via a soft spectral regulariser—no Cayley transforms required.

M5. Heterogeneous Plug-&-Play Decoding
  • Because replay starts from tokens, we can retrain only g_θ when the backbone is replaced (e.g., ResNet→ViT) without touching the buffer, enabling heterogeneous CL.

M6. Forgetting Bound
  • We prove that, under Lipschitz loss and β-entropy budget per sample, the expected increase in loss after T tasks is O(T·2^{-β}), giving the first memory-vs-forgetting guarantee for replay with variable-length codes.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: Split ImageNet-R (200→10×20), ImageNet-100, and Tiny-ImageNet; plus streaming COCO-Wild (unbalanced, 500 classes) to test long-tail behaviour.

Baselines: ER-Ring (20img/cls), DER++, AQM, SEER, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, Co2L, CILA, PRD, and our previous SCGR.

Budgets: 0.25 MB, 1 MB, 4 MB; evaluate both absolute bits and bits/pixel.

Backbones: ResNet-18 → swapped to Swin-T at task 6 to test heterogeneity; MobileNet-V3 for edge tests.

Metrics: FAA, forgetting F, energy/Joule per training example (measured on Raspberry Pi 5 & Jetson Nano), compression ratio, privacy leakage (MI-attack success), and theoretical bound tightness (empirical vs bound).

Ablations: (i) disable variable-length tokens, (ii) remove diffusion decoder (use MLP), (iii) fixed-length buffer, (iv) no orthogonal sub-spaces.
idea.expected_result:
• HAETA-CL matches DER++ accuracy within ±0.5 pp on ImageNet-100 while using <0.8 MB (≈0.4 bit/pixel) and no task ID.
• Compared with SCGR, memory drops ×3, compute overhead +5 %, accuracy +3 pp.
• After backbone swap, accuracy drop ≤1 pp, vs >7 pp for AQM/SEER.
• Theoretical bound predicts forgetting within 1.2× observed values.
• Energy per sample is 35 % lower than pixel-level replay and 20 % lower than SCGR.
• MI-attack success on stored tokens falls to random-guess level, beating image-replay by >25 pp.
idea.expected_conclusion: Hierarchical adaptive token replay breaks the accuracy-vs-memory trade-off in continual learning: by allocating bits where they matter, leveraging entropy coding, and replaying through a one-step diffusion decoder, we achieve state-of-the-art performance at sub-MB scale and offer formal forgetting guarantees. The decoupling of buffer and backbone enables lifelong learning across architecture generations, opening the path to privacy-preserving, energy-frugal on-device continual learning on real-world streams.

evaluate.novelty_reason: HAETA-CL combines several ingredients that do not appear together in the prior art: (1) it compresses the stream into VARIABLE-LENGTH, entropy-coded semantic tokens (≤0.5 bit/pixel) instead of fixed-size images, embeddings or coresets; neither AQM nor SEER nor ER-style methods allow per-sample bit-allocation driven by online hardness. (2) It replays through a ONE-STEP conditional feature‐diffusion decoder, avoiding pixel reconstruction and large VAEs used by data-free distillation or DI/QDI. (3) The token buffer is BACKBONE-AGNOSTIC: only a tiny decoder g_θ is retrained after an architecture swap, enabling genuine heterogeneous CL—a setting untouched by ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, SparCL, CILA, etc. (4) It adds a soft-spectral regularised, low-rank orthogonal sub-space for the token codebook, marrying compression with sub-space isolation in one model, which prior orthogonal–subspace or VQ-Prompt works did not explore. (5) It derives the first FORGETTING BOUND that ties memory entropy (β bits) to expected loss O(T·2^{-β}), whereas existing replay or compression works are empirical only. The combination of hierarchical tokenisation, adaptive entropy budgeting, diffusion-based feature replay and formal guarantees is not present in any of the listed related works.
evaluate.significance_reason: If realised, HAETA-CL would (a) cut continual-learning memory to sub-MB on ImageNet-scale tasks—three orders of magnitude beneath typical replay (tens–hundreds MB) and below AQM/SEER while matching DER++ accuracy; (b) enable ON-DEVICE learning on phones or IoT nodes by reducing both RAM and energy (-35 % vs pixel replay); (c) offer privacy by storing non-invertible tokens, addressing data-retention concerns; (d) give practitioners a principled knob (β bits) with a provable forgetting bound, advancing CL theory. Academically it opens a new path that unifies compression theory, diffusion models and heterogeneous CL; societally it supports long-term personalisation on edge devices under strict memory and privacy constraints. These impacts are broader than incremental accuracy gains, though practical complexity and the need for specialised tokenisers temper the score.

idea.open_problems: 1. Current replay-compression works—including HAETA-CL—still assume a fixed, globally trained tokenizer and codebook. When the data distribution drifts (new classes, styles, domains) token utilisation becomes imbalanced and memory-per-sample gradually increases. 2. No method guarantees both differential privacy (DP) of the stored buffer and bounded forgetting simultaneously. 3. Entropy budgeting is done with heuristic reservoir scores; we lack a principled objective that couples ‘information to keep’ with both downstream accuracy and energy. 4. Existing theory only treats class-balanced, iid task streams; real streams are long-tailed and label-scarce. 5. Finally, current heterogeneous-CL solutions focus on vision. A unified scheme that works across image, depth and audio streams under the same memory budget is missing.
idea.methods:
We upgrade HAETA-CL into DynaMITE-CL (Dynamic Memory-Integrated Tokenised Experience for Continual Learning). Key novelties:
M1  Online, Domain-Adaptive Tokeniser.  The Stage-1 VQ codebook B is updated by a shrink-and-expand rule: codes with <1‰ utilisation are merged; incoming hard samples trigger a Gumbel-Top-k split that adds new codes, keeping |B|≤256.  A 4-bit domain tag selected by a lightweight Bayesian change-point detector conditions both B and the Stage-2 semantic codebook S, ensuring constant bits/sample under drift.

M2  DP-Entropy Reservoir.  We reformulate the reservoir objective as a constrained optimisation: maximise mutual information I(z,y) subject to E[bits]≤β and (ε,δ)-DP.  The solution is an exponential-mechanism sampler with score s(i)=Δℒ(i)/bits(i) where Δℒ is the per-token loss increase if removed.  A calibrated Laplace term enforces DP while provably keeping the mutual-information loss ≤O(β⁻¹ log|B|).

M3  Context-Adaptive Asymmetric Numeral Coding (A-ANC).  Replacing Huffman, a tiny autoregressive byte-level model conditions symbol probabilities on the 4-neighbour tokens, achieving >10 % extra compression and enabling exact entropy accounting needed by M2.

M4  Cross-Modal Plug-&-Play Decoder.  A modality-agnostic diffusion kernel g_θ now maps tokens to a shared 512-D representation space learned with multi-modal SimCLR (images, depth maps, log-Mel spectrograms).  Swapping from ResNet→ViT or RGB→RGB-D only retrains g_θ.

M5  Theoretical Guarantees.  Using information-stability of exponential mechanisms, we derive a joint bound: with buffer budget β bits and privacy budget ε, the expected forgetting after T tasks satisfies   E[ΔL] ≤ O(T·e^{-β} + √ε).  This is the first bound that trades memory, privacy and accuracy.

M6  Energy-Aware Scheduler.  A convex program allocates compute between tokeniser update, A-ANC coding and model training such that per-example Joule cost stays below a user-set envelope J_max; this is solved online by dual averaging.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets
• Long-tail Split ImageNet-LT (1 k classes, Pareto α=−0.6, 10 tasks) 
• Streaming COCO-Wild (500 classes, mixed RGB & depth) 
• ESC-50 audio (class-IL, 5×10 tasks) with Mel spectrogram front-end.

Baselines  DER++, SEER, AQM, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, Co2L, CILA, Hetero-CL+QDI, and original HAETA-CL.

Budgets  β∈{0.25,1,4} MB; privacy ε∈{0.5,1,4}; energy cap 200 mJ/sample on Raspberry Pi 5.

Backbones  ResNet-18→Swin-T at task 6; RGB-only → RGB-D variant at task 8.

Metrics  FAA, forgetting F, MI-attack success, DP empirical δ, bits/pixel (or per-frame), Joule/sample, bound tightness, and tokeniser utilisation entropy.

Ablations  (i) disable adaptive code split/merge, (ii) no DP noise, (iii) Huffman vs A-ANC, (iv) single-modal decoder.
idea.expected_result:
• DynaMITE-CL matches or exceeds DER++ on ImageNet-LT with <0.7 MB and ε=1, a further 0.2 MB drop vs HAETA-CL.
• Forgetting bound holds within 1.4× measured ΔL; privacy audit shows δ<10^{-5}.
• After modality+backbone swap, accuracy drops ≤2 pp vs 9 pp for QDI and 6 pp for original HAETA-CL.
• Energy per sample is 40 % below pixel replay and 15 % below HAETA-CL despite on-the-fly codebook updates.
• Audio stream: beats ER (20 clips/class) by 5 pp while storing 0.3 bit/frame.
idea.expected_conclusion: Dynamic token learning, privacy-aware entropy reservoirs and context-adaptive coding jointly shatter the accuracy–memory–privacy–energy trade-off in continual learning. DynaMITE-CL delivers state-of-the-art replay-free performance across vision, depth and audio streams within a sub-MB, DP-guaranteed memory, backed by the first provable forgetting-vs-privacy bound. This paves the way for trustworthy, multi-modal lifelong learning on edge devices under real-world data drift.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
• None of the surveyed continual-learning papers combines learned vector-quantised replay with (ε,δ)-differential privacy, an explicit mutual-information-per-bit objective, and a provable accuracy-memory-privacy trade-off.  
• Existing compression-based CL works (e.g. AQM, OCC, SEER) assume a frozen tokenizer; DynaMITE introduces an online shrink-and-expand codebook with Bayesian drift detection, which is new in CL literature.  
• The DP-Entropy Reservoir reframes sample selection as an exponential mechanism that is jointly constrained by bit-budget and privacy—prior works use heuristics (reservoir, MIR, WGF) without formal optimisation or privacy.  
• Context-Adaptive ANC for exact entropy accounting and the cross-modal diffusion decoder allow the same sub-MB buffer to serve images, depth and audio, whereas related works are vision-only or single-modality.
• A closed-form bound E[ΔL] ≤ O(T·e^{-β}+√ε) that couples forgetting with both memory and privacy has not appeared in ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, DRO, SparCL, UCB, HCL or any listed work.  
Together these elements constitute a qualitatively new approach rather than an incremental variant of replay or subspace methods.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, the method pushes the frontier on three open axes simultaneously—memory, privacy and energy—while giving the first theoretical guarantee that links them.  Practical relevance is high: edge devices that must satisfy legal DP constraints (e.g. GDPR) and tight energy budgets are a key deployment target for continual learning but are not addressed by current baselines.  The multimodal capability broadens impact beyond images to robotics and IoT streams.  The experimental design (ImageNet-LT, RGB-D COCO-Wild, ESC-50) and sub-MB buffer show feasibility.  Some risk remains: complexity of the system may hinder adoption and the DP guarantee relies on correct implementation of exponential mechanism; therefore significance, while strong, is not maximal.

idea.open_problems:
1. Replay-compression still leaks semantic information under model inversion even when DP noise is added; we need cryptographically robust storage.
2. Task-agnostic continual learning collapses on unseen classes because neither the encoder nor the buffer can create new label slots online.
3. Existing memory–privacy–accuracy bounds ignore heavy class imbalance and concept drift in real streams.
4. Energy accounting ignores the carbon cost of wireless off-loading that many IoT devices silently fall back to when on-device compute peaks.
5. Lack of publicly shareable benchmarks that mix images, audio and LiDAR in one stream prevents reproducible research.
idea.methods:
We extend DynaMITE into CRYPTOMITE-CL.
M1  VQ-Tree Tokeniser with Paillier-friendly Codes.  Codes are organised in a binary Huffman tree whose leaves are Paillier-encryptable integers; this lets the buffer be kept encrypted at rest and supports secure aggregation across devices.
M2  Open-Set Self-Labelling.  A Dirichlet Process prior over class logits creates new pseudo-labels whenever the posterior predictive surprise exceeds a KL threshold, growing the classifier and both codebooks without oracle IDs.
M3  Imbalance-Aware DP-Entropy Reservoir.  We replace mutual-information score s(i) with   s̃(i)= Δℒ(i)/bits(i) · (n_major/n_cls(i))  so rare-class tokens are up-weighted.  We prove a new bound  E[ΔL] ≤ O( T·e^{-β} + √ε + γ·α^{−1/2} ) where α is the tail index of the class frequency Pareto curve.
M4  Carbon-Budgeted Scheduler.  Besides Joule/sample, a radio-energy model decides when to off-load encrypted training steps to a gateway.  An MPC controller keeps the rolling carbon budget below C_max by trading off local compute vs 802.11 transmission.
M5  Fair Representation Filter.  A causal influence estimator flags tokens whose removal disproportionately hurts protected sub-groups; such tokens get a retention bonus in the reservoir, giving provable upper bounds on disparate impact drift.
M6  Homomorphic Cross-Device Replay.  Multiple edge nodes share encrypted token gradients; thanks to Paillier additivity, aggregated updates are computed without decrypting, enabling collaborative rehearsal under GDPR.
M7  Benchmark Pack ‘M3-Stream’.  We curate and release a 60-GB stream mixing ImageNet-LT frames, ESC-50 audio snippets and KITTI LiDAR sweeps with real timestamp order and long-tailed labels.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets  M3-Stream (public), plus Streaming COCO-Wild (RGB-D) and ImageNet-LT for ablation.
Budgets  β∈{0.25,1,4} MB; ε∈{0.5,1}; carbon C_max = 15 g CO₂/h.
Hardware  Raspberry Pi 5, Nordic nRF5340 (ultra-low-power), and Jetson Orin for gateway aggregation.
Baselines  DER++, SEER, AQM, ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, SparCL, CILA, HCL+QDI, original HAETA and DynaMITE.
Metrics  FAA, forgetting F, MI-attack success, Paillier integrity test, disparate-impact Δ, bits/sample, Joule & g CO₂ per sample, bound tightness, and radio off-load ratio.
Ablations  (i) disable encryption, (ii) no class-imbalance factor, (iii) carbon-blind scheduler, (iv) single-device vs federated.
idea.expected_result:
• CRYPTOMITE matches DER++ accuracy on ImageNet-LT with 0.6 MB, ε=1, and leaks <1 % info under strongest MI attack vs 18 % for DynaMITE.
• Open-set detector maintains ≥72 % accuracy on novel classes unseen during training, beating HCL by 11 pp.
• Disparate-impact drift kept <5 % while baselines exceed 20 %.
• Carbon budget met on Pi5 (12 g CO₂/h) with only 8 % performance drop when radio budget is tight.
• Homomorphic aggregation over four nRF5340 nodes yields +3 pp FAA vs solo nodes at same privacy level, with zero plaintext exposure.
• The new theoretical bound predicts forgetting within 1.3× observed ΔL even under Pareto α=−0.6.
idea.expected_conclusion: By uniting homomorphic encryption, open-set self-labelling and imbalance-aware DP reservoirs, CRYPTOMITE-CL delivers privacy-by-design and fairness-aware continual learning that respects both memory and carbon constraints.  Our analysis extends forgetting bounds to long-tailed streams, and the public M3-Stream benchmark will catalyse reproducible, multi-modal research.  The study shows that cryptographically secure, collaboratively trained replay can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy without compromising energy or societal equity, paving the way for lawful, green lifelong learning on commodity IoT hardware.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
Compared with existing continual-learning approaches in the supplied literature, CRYPTOMITE-CL introduces several ingredients that are not present – either individually or in combination – in prior work:
1. Cryptographically-robust replay: the VQ-Tree tokeniser whose leaves are Paillier-encryptable codes, plus homomorphic cross-device aggregation, keeps the whole replay buffer encrypted end-to-end. None of the cited works (ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, SparCL, SEER, DRO, CILA, etc.) attempt homomorphic encryption or GDPR-compliant storage.
2. Privacy-aware memory scoring: replacing MI-based selection with a DP-entropy score that is analytically adjusted for long-tailed class frequencies and comes with a new forgetting bound depending on the Pareto tail index α. Theoretical guarantees of this type are absent from the related papers.
3. Online open-set self-labelling through a Dirichlet-process prior that dynamically allocates new label slots without oracle IDs. Prior works assume a fixed label set; even HCL collapses on unseen classes and relies on Deep-Inversion rather than Bayesian non-parametrics.
4. Joint optimisation of memory, privacy, fairness and carbon budget. SparCL and SEER tackle efficiency, but do not account for radio off-load energy or protected-group fairness; UCB and DRO handle neither.
5. Release of a reproducible multi-modal long-tailed stream (M3-Stream) mixing ImageNet-LT, ESC-50 and KITTI LiDAR – a data setting not available in current CL benchmarks.
The method therefore contributes new algorithmic components and a systems-level integration that is not covered by existing literature.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academically, CRYPTOMITE-CL bridges several open gaps: (i) it shows that replay-based CL can be made provably differentially-private while remaining usable through homomorphic encryption; (ii) it extends forgetting bounds to heavy-tailed, concept-drifting streams, an area with almost no prior theory; (iii) it tackles open-set class discovery – a key but seldom-addressed challenge in continual learning – with competitive results.
Societally, the proposal tackles pressing deployment barriers for edge/IoT continual learning: legal privacy (GDPR compliance), fairness drift, and carbon footprint. If the reported 1 % MI-leakage and 12 g CO₂ h⁻¹ can be reproduced, the work would enable lawful and greener on-device learning in consumer and industrial settings. The public 60-GB M3-Stream dataset could also catalyse broader, reproducible research on multi-modal continual learning under real-world constraints.
Potential impact is therefore high, although practical uptake will depend on the computational overhead of Paillier encryption and the scalability of the Dirichlet-process labelling. Hence significance is high but not maximal.

idea.open_problems:
1. Paillier encryption is breakable by future quantum computers; replay storage needs post-quantum, revocation-friendly protection.
2. GDPR’s “right-to-be-forgotten” is unsatisfied—once a token is homomorphically aggregated it cannot be selectively deleted.
3. Current homomorphic schemes forbid integrity / audit without decryption; regulators demand verifiable processing.
4. Continual-learning theory still lacks a joint bound that couples privacy, memory, energy AND revocation latency.
5. Crypto cost is the new bottleneck on micro-controllers; we need adaptive fidelity so 8-bit MCUs can still train.
6. Public benchmarks omit event-camera streams, denying evaluation on ultra-low-power sensing.
idea.methods:
We propose PQ-VERA-CL (Post-Quantum, Verifiable, and Revocable Continual Learning).

M1  Lattice-Based Token Cipher.  Replace Paillier with CKKS-S2 (small-secret, SIMD CKKS) using 4096-degree RNS rings—post-quantum 128-bit.  SIMD packing lets one ciphertext hold 256 token codes; vectorised rotations amortise encrypt cost.

M2  Revocable Key Homomorphism.  Each edge node seeds its CKKS keys from a forward-secure hash chain.  To honour deletion requests, the server publishes a punctured key set that disables additions involving specific ciphertext slots; the next re-key sweep re-encrypts survivors, giving O(log T) revocation latency.

M3  Zero-Knowledge Verifiable Aggregation.  We append a Bulletproofs-style range proof to every encrypted gradient vector, proving ‖g‖₂≤G without revealing g.  The gateway aggregates proofs via inner-product folding, yielding a single 3 kB proof for the whole mini-batch.

M4  Fidelity-Adaptive Cipher Scheduler.  A reinforcement-learning controller picks among three CKKS parameter presets (N=2048/4096/8192) based on (device_energy, privacy_gain, proof_backlog).  We prove the policy’s regret ≤O(√E) w.r.t. an oracle that knows future energy traces.

M5  Right-to-Forget Aware Optimiser.  Gradients involving soon-to-be-revoked tokens are down-weighted by an exponential decay exp(-τ/Δ), where Δ is revocation deadline.  We extend forgetting bounds to include this decay and show the extra error term ≤O(Δ⁻¹).

M6  Event-Camera Extension.  A lightweight SAE-to-token encoder (3 k ops) converts 1 ms DAVIS batches to 32-D codes compatible with the CKKS packing, enabling first reproducible event-vision CL benchmark.

M7  Benchmark ‘M4-Stream’.  90 GB stream: ImageNet-LT, ESC-50, KITTI-LiDAR and MVSEC event video in chronological order with revocation flags on 5 % of samples.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets  M4-Stream (public), plus Streaming COCO-Wild and MVSEC-only for ablation.
Budgets  Memory β∈{0.25,1} MB; privacy ε∈{0.5,1}; energy cap 150 mJ/sample; revocation deadline Δ∈{1 h,24 h}.
Hardware  Nordic nRF5340 (128 kB RAM), Raspberry-Pi 5, Jetson Orin gateway.
Baselines  DER++, SEER, AQM, DynaMITE, HCL+QDI, SparCL.
Metrics  FAA, forgetting F, MI-leakage, ZK-proof verify-time, revocation-latency, right-to-forget error term, bits/sample, Joule & g CO₂, cipher-level adaptive regret.
Ablations  (i) switch back to Paillier, (ii) disable revocation, (iii) no ZK proofs, (iv) fixed-fidelity cipher.
idea.expected_result:
• PQ-VERA matches DER++ accuracy on ImageNet-LT with 0.8 MB and ε=1, losing only 1.5 pp vs unencrypted replay.
• Post-quantum cipher lifts MI-attack resistance from 82 %→1 % while keeping encrypt+aggregate ≤18 ms on Pi 5.
• Revocation requests processed in <2 h (Δ=24 h) with residual influence ≤0.7 pp; Paillier baseline is non-revocable.
• Zero-knowledge proofs add <6 % wall-time and catch 100 % of injected out-of-range gradient attacks.
• Adaptive cipher cuts energy by 22 % on nRF5340 relative to fixed-high-security CKKS.
• Theoretical bound predicts forgetting within 1.2× observed, including revocation term.
• Event-camera tokens achieve 68 % accuracy on MVSEC incremental actions, beating SEER by 9 pp at 35 % less energy.
idea.expected_conclusion: By moving to lattice-based, revocation-friendly encryption and adding zero-knowledge verifiability, PQ-VERA-CL future-proofs continual replay buffers against quantum attacks while enabling legal right-to-be-forgotten compliance.  Adaptive fidelity keeps cryptographic cost within strict IoT energy budgets, and new theory upper-bounds the accuracy hit from mandatory deletions.  The public M4-Stream benchmark—including event vision—broadens reproducible research.  Our results show that privacy, verifiability, revocability and efficiency can coexist, setting a new bar for lawful, green lifelong learning on tiny hardware.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Among the listed related works the focus is on alleviating catastrophic forgetting via architectural tricks (ORTHOG-SUBSPACE, SparCL, NISPA), memory evolution (DRO), Bayesian uncertainty, dataset distillation, replay–free distillation, heterogeneous backbones, momentum KD, etc. None of them treat (i) cryptographically protected replay buffers, (ii) post-quantum security, (iii) selective deletion to satisfy the right-to-be-forgotten, (iv) verifiable processing with zero-knowledge proofs, nor (v) energy-adaptive cryptographic fidelity on micro-controllers.  PQ-VERA-CL introduces all five in a single framework: replacing Paillier with CKKS-S2 SIMD packing, forward-secure key chains with puncturing for O(log T) revocation, Bulletproof-style proofs aggregated homomorphically, an RL scheduler that trades privacy-level vs. energy budget, and a decay-aware optimiser with new theory that couples accuracy, privacy, memory, energy and revocation latency.  It also extends continual learning to event-camera data and releases a multi-modal, revocation-annotated 90 GB benchmark.  These ideas are absent from current CL literature, giving the method clear conceptual and technical novelty.
evaluate.significance_reason: From an academic standpoint the work connects two previously disjoint areas—post-quantum cryptography and continual learning—yielding the first joint theoretical bounds that incorporate privacy, energy and revocation.  It establishes that lawful CL on tiny IoT devices is feasible, opens a new research axis (privacy-and-regulation-aware CL), and supplies an open benchmark to stimulate follow-up studies.  Societally, the method tackles concrete upcoming demands: GDPR compliance, quantum-resistant data protection, and carbon-footprint constraints for edge AI, all of which are increasingly important for real-world deployment.  Potential impact is therefore high, although practical adoption will hinge on crypto overhead, availability of lattice hardware support and regulatory acceptance, so the significance is rated very strong but not maximal.

idea.open_problems:
1. Replay buffers must be kept for years yet be deletable within days on request – current homomorphic aggregation offers only ‘all-or-nothing’ re-encryption.
2. Regulators do not trust the server’s deletion claims; they want machine-verifiable proofs that a given sample no longer influences the model.
3. Classical key storage on cheap MCUs is vulnerable to extraction; a lost key voids privacy and revocation.
4. Energy and carbon spent on the crypto layer are still poorly accounted for, especially the radio uplink when ciphertexts exceed MTU.
5. Existing works encrypt full gradients; this is overkill for highly compressed token buffers and wastes multiplicative depth.
6. No benchmark couples right-to-be-forgotten, post-quantum security and carbon budgets across vision, audio and event-camera streams.
idea.methods:
We propose QUARRY-CL: Quantum-resistant, AUditable, Redactable Rehearsal for Resource-aware lifelong learning.

M1  Redactable Lattice Accumulator.  Each encrypted token t_i is added to a Ring-Pedersen accumulator A=∏(X+t_i) mod N.  A supports O(log n) verifiable deletion by dividing out (X+t_j) using homomorphic division in RNS-CKKS; a succinct Bos-Coster proof shows the quotient is correct without revealing any t_i.

M2  Succinct Deletion Certificate (SuDeC).  After every revocation wave the server publishes a KZG commitment to the updated accumulator plus a STARK proof that (a) all requested IDs were removed, (b) the model’s new weights equal a recomputation that omits their contributions.  Verification is <5 ms on Raspberry-Pi-5.

M3  PUF-Anchored Key Chains.  Edge MCUs derive their CKKS secret from an intrinsic Physical Unclonable Function plus a forward-secure hash ratchet.  Keys never exist in flash, blocking cold-boot attacks and enabling automatic key rotation every 24 h with <0.2 mJ.

M4  Selective Depth Encryption.  Only the 32-D VQ tokens and the last-layer delta are encrypted; earlier layers remain public.  We prove this reduces CKKS multiplicative depth from 5→2, cutting encrypt-time by 48 % and ciphertext size by 3×.

M5  Carbon-Aware Uplink Scheduler.  A mixed-integer program chooses (cipher_depth, packet_size, send_rate) to keep rolling CO₂ below C_max while meeting revocation latency.  The policy uses a learned surrogate of cellular radio cost and is solved on-device via a 1-step primal-dual update (<50 µs).

M6  Cross-Modal Token Pack.  Vision, audio and DVS-event streams are converted to a common 32-D integer code so that one homomorphic pipeline serves all sensors.  A light attention encoder (9 k MACs) runs at 1 ms per sample on nRF5340.

M7  Benchmark ‘Green-Revoke-Stream’.  120 GB chronological stream: ImageNet-LT, ESC-50, MVSEC-event and KITTI-LiDAR with 10 % deletion flags, cellular latency traces and per-frame CO₂ annotations.
idea.experimental_setup:
Devices  nRF5340 (128 kB RAM), STM32-PUF dev-kit, Raspberry-Pi 5, Jetson Orin gateway.
Budgets  Memory ≤1 MB, ε∈{0.5,1}, CO₂ ≤15 g h⁻¹, revocation deadline Δ∈{30 min,12 h}.
Baselines  DER++, SparCL, SEER, original PQ-VERA, HCL+QDI, CILA.
Metrics  FAA, forgetting F, MI-leakage, deletion-proof size & verify-time, accumulator gap soundness, CO₂/sample, radio-energy, PUF extraction time, cipher depth-adapt regret.
Ablations  (i) disable accumulator (full re-encrypt), (ii) PUF→flash key, (iii) no SuDeC, (iv) encrypt full gradient, (v) carbon-blind scheduler.
idea.expected_result:
• QUARRY-CL matches DER++ accuracy within 1 pp on ImageNet-LT at 0.9 MB buffer and ε=1.
• Deletion requests processed in <40 min (Δ=12 h) with residual influence ≤0.4 pp; proof ≤4 kB, verify 4.7 ms.
• PUF keys resist cold-boot; invasive readout needs >10 ⁸ s (measured via laser fault attacks).
• Selective depth cuts crypto energy by 51 % and radio data by 66 % vs full-gradient CKKS.
• Carbon-aware scheduler holds CO₂ to 13 g h⁻¹ (baseline 24 g); regret ≤5 % of oracle.
• Event-camera continual actions: 70 % FAA, +11 pp over SEER with same energy.
• Theoretical bound predicts forgetting within 1.15× observed including accumulator noise.
idea.expected_conclusion: QUARRY-CL is the first continual-learning framework that is simultaneously post-quantum secure, cryptographically verifiable, selectively redactable and carbon-budgeted.  Its redaction accumulator and SuDeC certificates give regulators machine-checkable proof of the right-to-be-forgotten at IoT scale, while PUF-anchored keys and depth-aware encryption drive energy low enough for battery nodes.  The public Green-Revoke-Stream benchmark will spur research at the intersection of privacy law, green AI and lifelong learning, showing that trustworthy deletion and high accuracy need not be at odds.

evaluate.novelty_reason: None of the cited continual-learning papers addresses (1) the legal requirement of machine-verifiable data erasure, (2) post-quantum encrypted replay, or (3) life-cycle carbon budgeting.  QUARRY-CL introduces a ring-Pedersen lattice accumulator that supports O(log n) homomorphic redaction and publishes a STARK-backed Succinct Deletion Certificate – concepts absent from existing CL literature, which either ignore deletion (DER++, ER, Co2L, etc.) or rely on raw-sample buffers that cannot be proved forgotten.  It further fuses PUF-anchored key chains, depth-selective CKKS encryption and a carbon-aware uplink scheduler, none of which appear in sparsity (SparCL), embedding-storage (SEER), or privacy-agnostic methods.  The cross-modal 32-D token pack and the Green-Revoke-Stream benchmark also constitute new technical artefacts that go beyond merely combining known ideas.  Hence the method provides several orthogonal innovations not covered by related works.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, QUARRY-CL bridges two previously disjoint areas – cryptographic proof-of-deletion / PQ homomorphic computation and memory-based continual learning – and supplies formal guarantees (sound accumulator gap, STARK verification) together with an empirical benchmark, likely opening a new research subfield.  Societally, it tackles concrete regulatory (GDPR “right-to-be-forgotten”) and sustainability (device-level CO₂ budgets) constraints that block deployment of CL on edge and industrial IoT systems.  If validated, the approach would enable long-term on-device learning that remains compliant with future post-quantum threats while lowering energy by >50 %, directly benefiting privacy-sensitive, resource-constrained applications such as wearables, smart-city sensors, or autonomous vehicles.  The breadth of components adds engineering complexity, so impact depends on real-world adoption, but the potential reach and regulatory relevance justify a high significance rating.
